newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian business dismayed at Kabariti departure.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian business dismayed at Kabariti departure.

text.p: Jordanian economists and businessmen were disappointed on Wednesday with King Hussein's decision to dismiss reformist Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti.

They said at best the decision meant a hiatus in free market economic reforms as the new government of Abdul-Salam al-Majali, whose previous administration showed little sign of pioneering economic initiatives, found its feet.
And Majali faced a tough task translating his good relations with Israel and Iraq into better trade with Jordan's neighbours, they said.

"We were looking for someone with initiative in economic affairs," said the manager of one Amman investment company. "Majali was in charge during the peace negotiations (with Israel) but we saw little accomplished locally under his government."
"Anyone who steps in right now will need time, and this is a delay which right now we cannot handle," he said. "Everyone is telling Jordan that we are taking too long with changes."

Kabariti, appointed in early 1996 with a mandate including wide-ranging economic and administrative reforms, pushed through tough IMF-backed measures like bread subsidy cuts which led to riots in August and calls for his resignation.
But his "white revolution" got snarled up in bureaucracy.
New laws reforming private companies, customs duties and the Amman stock exchange were held up in parliament. And plans for privatisation have yet to take off.
"If Majali wants to march ahead with the privatisation programme he will have to take time first to see what was going on," said the investment manager.
A number of businessmen praised Majali as a "cool thinker" who would give their case a fair hearing.
"Majali is a man who listens and he does respond to the business community," said Hamdi Tabaa, head of the Jordan Business Association.
Tabaa said he hoped Jordan under Majali would be able to increase its exports to Iraq, Jordan's biggest trade partner.
"Under his first cabinet there was more trade with Iraq than we have today," Tabaa added.

But a Jordanian banker said Majali would struggle to turn his good ties with Baghdad -- a stark contrast with Kabariti who was seen as spearheading Jordan's turn against President Saddam Hussein in 1995 -- into fresh business opportunities.
"The Iraqi market is not like it was before, it's not about personal ties," he said. "Now it's monitored by the United Nations and everything has to be officially tendered."
Most businessmen said they would reserve judgement on Majali's appointment until he announced his cabinet, expected to include members of the previous government.
But one declined to get excited by the flurry of changes Majali was expected to make, citing King Hussein's fondness for frequent reshuffles.
"In Jordan we change governments like we change clothes," he said.
